title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.5.1-c15, 4.5.1-c03, 4.5.1-c04, 4.5.1-c17. Clues: 4.5.1-c15 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.1-c03 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.1-c04 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.5.1-c17 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.5.1-q16, 4.5.1-q17, 4.5.1-q18, 4.5.1-q19, 4.5.1-q20, 4.5.1-q21, 4.5.1-q22, 4.5.1-q23, 4.5.1-q24, 4.5.1-q25, 4.5.1-q26, 4.5.1-q27.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Activation energy
items.clue: The minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react.

items.label: Exothermic reaction
items.clue: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases.

items.label: Endothermic reaction
items.clue: A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

items.label: Overall energy change
items.clue: The difference in energy between the reactants and the products, shown on a reaction profile and, at higher tier, calculated from bond energies.

questions.stem: Two reactant particles collide with each other but no reaction takes place. What is the reason?

options.text: Every collision must react, so this cannot happen.
They collided with less than the energy given out here.
They collided with too little energy to react.
The reaction is exothermic, so no energy is needed.

questions.explanation: Reactions occur only when particles collide with sufficient energy; a collision below the activation energy simply bounces apart.

questions.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: the minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react
the height of the peak measured from the bottom axis of the diagram
the total amount of energy the reaction gives out overall
the energy released whenever two reactant particles collide

questions.explanation: This is the specification's definition of the activation energy, word for word in substance.

questions.stem: Which set of quantities can be shown on a reaction profile?

options.text: the temperature change, provided it is large enough to count as a real energy transfer
the relative energies of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change
the activation energy on its own, because the products are not marked anywhere on the diagram
the rise in temperature, showing the energy that the chemicals have taken in

questions.explanation: These are precisely the three things the specification says a reaction profile can be used to show.

questions.stem: A student draws a reaction profile for an endothermic reaction. Which description of the drawing is correct?

options.text: The products line lies below the reactants, joined by a curve with a peak.
A straight sloping line runs from the reactants line up to the products.
The products line lies above the reactants, joined by a curved peak.
The top of the curve is level with the products line on the right.

questions.explanation: Endothermic products are higher in energy than the reactants, and the specification asks for a curved line passing over the activation energy peak.

questions.stem: A reaction profile shows the products at a lower energy than the reactants. What does this tell you about the reaction?

options.text: It is endothermic and takes in energy overall.
It is exothermic only if the peak is low.
It cannot happen, as products must be higher.
It is exothermic and gives out energy.

questions.explanation: Products lower than reactants means the chemicals have lost energy, and that energy has gone to the surroundings.

questions.stem: Why must colliding particles have at least the activation energy?

options.text: because it is the energy the reaction gives to the surroundings
because it is the energy that is needed for the reaction to occur
because it is only needed when a reaction is endothermic
because it is the energy needed to make particles collide

questions.explanation: The specification puts it in exactly these terms: the activation energy is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.

questions.stem: During a chemical reaction, what happens to the bonds in the reactants?

options.text: Energy is released as each one of them breaks.
They break with no energy change at all.
Energy must be supplied so that they break.
They break, and forming new bonds also takes energy.

questions.explanation: The specification states that energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.

questions.stem: What happens to energy when the bonds in the products are formed?

options.text: Energy is released only if it is exothermic.
Energy must be supplied to make them form.
Energy is stored and none gets out.
Energy is released as these bonds form.

questions.explanation: The specification states that energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.

questions.stem: A student is given a table of bond energies for a reaction. What can these values be used to calculate?

options.text: the energy taken in breaking bonds and released forming them
the total energy of the reaction, by adding up every value in the table
the number of bonds broken and the number of bonds formed in total
the temperature rise, showing the energy the chemicals take in

questions.explanation: Bond energies give both sums the specification names: the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.

questions.stem: How is the overall energy change of a reaction found from bond energies?

options.text: the sum of the energy released forming bonds minus the sum needed to break
the sum of the energy needed to break bonds added to the sum released
the sum of the energy needed to break bonds minus the sum released forming bonds
the number of bonds broken subtracted from the number of bonds made

questions.explanation: This is the specification's definition of the overall energy change: the difference between the two sums, taken in that order.

questions.stem: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is the overall energy change?

options.text: +1540 kJ/mol, adding all the values up
+184 kJ/mol, so it is endothermic
+247 kJ/mol, using one H-Cl bond
-184 kJ/mol, so this is exothermic

questions.explanation: Breaking: 436 + 242 = 678. Forming: 2 x 431 = 862. Overall energy change = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol, so energy is given out.

questions.stem: In an exothermic reaction, how do the two bond energy sums compare?

options.text: Forming new bonds releases more than breaking bonds needs.
Breaking existing bonds needs more than forming new bonds gives out.
More bonds are formed in the products than are broken overall.
The two sums are equal, so no energy is left over here.

questions.explanation: The specification states that in an exothermic reaction the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds.
